Final E3000 in-Ear Headphones, Hi-Fi Sound Quality, Hires Certified, Award Winning, Stainless Steel Housing, 3.5mm Standard Plug, Natural Sound with Extended Bass, Designed in Japan I am not shy about returning headphones I don't like but these are KEEPERS. This might be the happiest I've been with some earphones since my beloved Nuforce NE-700X. But to be fair those cost $90 in 2014.

Update after 2 weeks of use:

I went to a larger tip and now they don't sit as far in my ear. The bass and soundstage both improved with more air around the instruments. I really like these. I don't find myself thinking oh they do this, or they don't do that with regard to sound. The just play the music. That little TINY bit of graininess is gone with some break in I guess. While I don't listen to Metal or EDM they handle all genres of music well and handle more complex music like rock well compared to others I have tried. They come with 4 size tips so finding the right size is easier compared to pairs that only come with 3 size tips. The tips grip the nozzle really well but still come off and go on pretty easily. They come with some really small ear hooks but I haven't tried them yet. There is no listening fatigue yet they are still pretty accurate. They do not go really loud but they do go loud enough for me.I haven't played with EQ much because I haven't felt the need. Wires are thin and tangle pretty easily and don't untangle very easily. I have not noticed any microphonics. Of course, I'd like to have $100 buds but for $55 dollars they hit my nice but I won't cry if I lose them price point.

===========================================
Original review

They are not even broken in yet (and they don't need it) but my only real complaint and it's nitpicky, but they have a touch of graininess. But nowhere near as much as the Carbo Tenor. These are very neutra with decent detail while never being too bright. There is nice seperation between instruments but not much of a soundstage but there is nice amount of 'air' around the intruments. They do not have a lot of extension but they are not bass shy like the Carbo Tenor were. Drums sound natural, again not like the Carbo Tenor where they sounded more like carboard boxes.

They are very light so they very comfortable. (I like straight earphones the best) The default tips fit me the best which is a nice change for me. There is next to no strain relief on the earphones as you can see in the picture so if you are hard on headphones, maybe consider other phones. on the good side the lack of strain relief makes them very comfortable worn wire up which i want for the gym. They have vents on the back so I doubt that isolation is very good for in-ear phones.

In summary these are nuetral sounding with out any of the 'problems' of hifi. They are never over sibilant and they do not punish badly recorded songs or when listening to low bit rate stuff like pandora. I would call them fun for working out but they are not too dry if the quality of the music is what you want. They are not going to impress anyone or give you an eargasm when listening to your best music. But at $54 I'm extemely please with them and for me are a big step up from the Carbo Tenor unless you are impressed by a forward/blaring sound.

Logitech MX Vertical Wireless Mouse – Advanced Ergonomic Design Reduces Muscle Strain, Control and Move Content Between 3 Windows and Apple Computers (Bluetooth or USB), Rechargeable, Graphite I have a couple of vertical mice that I use with my various computer systems, and they really do help with wrist fatigue and pressure. I also have a very nice Logitech MX Ergo trackball which is my go-to device for all of my systems. With Logitech releasing this vertical mouse, I was very optimistic that I would have the perfect solution. I was sorely disappointed. This is the worst Logitech device I have used and I can’t recommend it.

I’ll start with the good aspects of it, and then I will get into what isn’t so good.

This device can be connected via wireless USB or by Bluetooth. This is handy for when you want to use multiple systems and want to connect to them, in different ways. If you already have another wireless Logitech device, it can connect to the receiver for that device, reducing the number of wireless ports required. It connects well through either method and I have been able to move it between systems just with the press of the connection button on top.

In operation, it seems to work well as a pointing device. I will say that if you are not used to working with a vertical mouse there is a learning curve that is involved and you will be very frustrated while you make the adjustment. The movement isn’t hard – it’s working with the buttons which even though are worked with the same fingers they feel unnatural at first. This is a problem with all vertical mice, not just this one.

It is rechargeable, meaning no more batteries, and it holds a charge for a good while. I like mice and keyboards that don’t need batteries as in the very long term it saves money. (Logitech has a solar keyboard that is phenomenal and never needs to be plugged in at all – great device.)

I have three main issues with this vertical mouse. The first is the build quality. It feels very lightweight and cheap, and I would call it fragile. It is supposed to be light and maneuverable so it’s easy to use, but it’s so much so that it has a very cheap feel to it that is unsettling. Second, this is a HUGE mouse which for me is great but for most people is unworkable. It fits my hand very well, but I have hands like a gorilla. My wife tried it and found it to be completely unusable because she couldn’t work the buttons well at all due to the size. Finally, this is a very expensive peripheral compared to other vertical mice I have used that I actually prefer. This vertical mouse presently sells here for about $100. I have one that cost around $25 at the time I bought it, feels more solid and is easier to use. My wife and I compared the Logitech vertical mouse with my cheaper one, and we both agreed that the less expensive one was easier to handle and worked just as well. The only thing I lose with the cheaper mouse is Bluetooth connectivity, which in my case is not a deal breaker.

I wish I could rate this mouse more highly but I just can’t. It’s expensive, feels cheap and just isn’t made to fit smaller hands (and usually, it’s a challenge finding mice for larger hands). It’s worth consideration if you need a mouse that can be easily transitioned between wireless and Bluetooth, but if you just need to use it with one system I’d recommend researching other options before making a purchase.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech MX Vertical Wireless Mouse – Advanced Ergonomic Design Reduces Muscle Strain, Control and Move Content Between 3 Windows and Apple Computers (Bluetooth or USB), Rechargeable, Graphite

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Performance MX Wireless Mouse (DISCONTINUED and Replaced by MX Master 2S) howdy y'all,

i bought this mouse to replace my logitech mx1100 cordless mouse. that one finally had the left mouse button start doing the dreaded false double click. it lasted several years, so i was not seriously annoyed. [*grin*]

for those coming from an mx1100, here are differences i noticed ...
- the mx1100 had the hump in the center instead of towards the back, so the main mouse buttons were shorter
this makes the mouse seem really rather too long. i am unsure if that will bother me once i use the new one for a while.

- the mx1100 had less of a slant to the right so that my hand sat a bit closer to level
the new one is more comfy for my very right-handed self.

- the mx1100 mouse wheel projected a tad more
combined with the sharp slant, the new mouse wheel feels like it is tilted the wrong way. it isn't, but i keep finding my finger on the right edge of the wheel instead of directly on the wheel.

- the mx1100 mouse wheel had a more pronounced side-move feel
the new mouse is very subtle. i liked the distinct feel of the older one when it toggled the side-move "button" function of the mouse wheel. of course, i like clicky keyboards, too ... [*grin*]

- the mx1100 had the upper thumb buttons just below the upper left edge
the new mouse has them on a surface that slants very sharply down to the left from the left edge. it makes the reach to the forward/back buttons a tad less comfy. combine that with a taper on those two buttons and i have found myself looking to see where the darned buttons went. they are also a tad more to the front of the mouse.
these admittedly annoying things that will likely fade out of my attention with use.

- the mx1100 used two AA rechargeable batteries
the new mouse uses one. since i use a lot of battery powered devices, i have a battery charger and several spares on hand. that means i will likely not use the usb charging function very often. still, one AA is better than having to charge two! [*grin*]

- the mx1100 had a larger usb wireless adapter
the new one is quite tiny! it works well - i put it on the back of my system among the tangle of wires that connect to other things and have had no reception problems.

*****
the parts list says there otta be a driver cd included. _not_ so! [*sigh ...*] you are referred to their download site if you want to use any of the extended functions or buttons. the performance mx has a $100 recommended price and there is no excuse to cheap out like that. thankfully, win7x32 has basic mouse support for the standard buttons, the mouse wheel, and the back/forward buttons.

this is a /_serious_/ fubar and i almost subtracted a star from my rating because of it.
*****

i suspect that folks with short hands will have problems with this mouse, but i am getting used to it already. i'm 6'1" and my hand is 7.5" from base to middle finger tip. not a _large_ hand, but not short.

*****
rated a THREE since it does what i expected - no more and no less. still, i came very close to rating this a two for not including the cd.

take care,
lee
text_fidelity_b: Logitech Performance MX Wireless Mouse (DISCONTINUED and Replaced by MX Master 2S)

CanaKit Raspberry Pi 3 Complete Starter Kit - 32 GB Edition This is a very complete kit and does contain everything you need to setup a Raspberry Pi 3. Yes, the op system installs easily and, with luck, you can be up and running in less than an hour. So, why the 2 stars?

It gets 2 stars because the Raspberry Pi is probably one of the most frustrating devices I've ever tried to put to any real use. For example, I wanted to set it up so I could use a VNC server on the Pi and a VNC client on my Mac (OS X El Capitan). After three days of almost non-stop failures, I'm sick of this thing. Researching how to get this task done leads you down a black hole of internet articles and posts on the Raspberry Pi site, most of that give different instructions, use different commands, tell you which files to edit and what to put in them, and almost none work, period!

The core problem rests squarely on the Raspberry Pi organization. Their own website is full of conflicting posts on how to do just about anything beyond a basic setup. Few, if any posts state which model of Pi is being referenced, and many bear no date. All in all, it's a very frustrating experience and, while I like to tinker with these things, a little success is required once in a while to keep me chugging along. I think I'm done with this thing. I had hoped it would finally be a Linux for the rest of us. Unfortunately, it's just as convoluted and difficult to use as any version of Linux out there (my opinion).

However, if you're looking to explore the Pi, this kit has everything you need to do a basic setup of Linux. And, should you want to use it as a web server, file server, media server, you're really on your own. Drink lots of coffee and plan to pull our lots of hair.
text_fidelity_b: CanaKit Raspberry Pi 3 Complete Starter Kit - 32 GB Edition

There’s a channel called PC Monkey & he has videos to walk you through all the troubleshooting for this problem. I tried all of the easy ones, but none worked. I ended up following his instructions for a fresh install of Windows from a USB - and lo and behold the laptop is like new again! It only took about 30 minutes to complete the process, and you will need another computer + a flash drive to download the install file.

I probably will not buy another Lenovo after this experience. I hope this review helps someone else who runs into the same problem.

BUGANI Bluetooth Speakers, M83 Speaker IPX6 Waterproof Portable LargeWireless Speaker,Bluetooth 5.2, Wireless Two Pairing,24H Playtime,Suitable for Family Gatherings and Outdoor Bluetooth Speaker I ordered this for the higher wattage and on my primary phone, it does get quite loud; but on my Dex device, it's maxed out is equivalent to about 50% volume on a 10W speaker.
I used a dB meter that was about 6ft away with the speaker pointed towards the meter. At max volume on my main phone (fold3) and at 150% volume, I was getting a consistent mid-90s dB for melody and lyrics, with peaks up to 109dB. On my other device (Note 10+), also at 150%, it was pulling about 70 dB on TV dialogue. I did try testing it with a volume booster, and even with only 110% (on top of the 150%) it was beginning to distort.
I played the TV audio for about 16hrs at moderate and 8hrs on low, and it was reading as still having 70% battery. But after only a few hours of moderate-high volume music, that 70% was gone and it died.
The sound quality is quite good with a warm tone. The highs are clear and the bass is better than I expected for there not to be a dedicated bass cone.
Despite appearances, I think the best use for this will be background music - not too loud will keep it playing all day & night and it will provide a much cleaner and richer sound than a small speaker at similar volume.

text_fidelity_a:
Brainwavz S5 IEM Noise Isolating Earphones with Clearwavz Remote and Microphone for iPhone iPad iPod I’m a big fan of the Brainwavz S1 (actually all of their headphones – have yet to be disappointed with any of their products). The S1 has been my main set for active use (e.g., workouts, runs, etc.) since the flat cable is very durable and resistant to tangles. The S5 keeps all the good features of the S1 and adds to it – the sound quality is richer and better defined.

That’s not to say the S1 sounds poor – they are quite good, in fact. But the S5 are better. The highs are better defined and the midrange has more punch to it. The bass comes through clearly without moving into the harsh territory when the volume is pushed (as the S1s can do). The overall sound quality is very pleasing.

The build quality seems solid – as solid as the S1 or better. I love the flat cable! I know that’s something that is not appreciated by everyone, but for me it’s been working out wonderfully. Although this (as most other Brainwavz headsets) comes with an excellent hard shell case, I usually tote my earbuds wrapped around my mp3 player in my pocket. Easy to carry; very stressful on the cables and can lead to tangles with round wires. Flat wires, especially those with a thick jacket such as these, survive that abuse with zero problems.

The earbuds themselves are more sleekly shaped than the “can” style of the S1.

Comfort is in line with the customary Brainwavz style, which is to say it’s outstanding. It comes with a wide range of tips to fit pretty much any ear, plus the Comply foam tips (which are my favorite). If fitted properly you end up with zero ear irritation plus excellent sound isolation and bass response.

These are an over-the-ear design much like the S1. I never used that design prior to the S1 and it did take me a little time to get accustomed to it. It became second nature quickly, and the design is a lot more stable when exercising than the conventional in-ear design.

These are more expensive than the S1, but you can hear the difference in price. Still, if you’re looking to keep the cost down a bit, the S1 is an excellent performer as well.

Great sound, great comfort, wonderful cable design, and it comes with a solidly made case and lots of eartips. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Brainwavz S5 IEM Noise Isolating Earphones with Clearwavz Remote and Microphone for iPhone iPad iPod

text_fidelity_a:
Renegade Concepts: Lap PRO - Stand/Caddy Universal Beanbag Lap Stand Tablet Accessory for iPad 1, iPad 2, iPad 3, iPad 4, Acer, Nexus & All Android Tablets, E-Readers, Books & Google Devices (Blue) The LAP PRO universal tablet stand doesn't work very well with my Kindle Fire HD 8.9" Wi-Fi tablet. The stand consists of a very firm, 18-inch wide, cylindrical pillow with a soft handle that doubles as a sort of tray for the tablet. Because there is no frame to hold the tablet securely, the tablet must be set carefully into the handle-tray, and then the tablet simply leans against the pillow for support. However, the tablet is very easily dislodged from the tray, even when the stand is sitting on a flat tabletop.

Out of the box, the LAP PRO holds the 8.9" Kindle Fire HD tablet at a near-vertical angle that is uncomfortable for viewing or for using a stylus on the touch screen. There is a sheet packed with the pillow that says: "Your LAP PRO has come slightly over filled intentionally, which may interfere with some functions. This will change in time. This is to ensure it will perform properly and last longer after it breaks in. The fabric will stretch and the beans settle from use." However, this is not really a beanbag stand. The pillow is filled with something that feels like medium-fine sand (not beans). Also, the pillow is too firm to accommodate its shape to an uneven surface the way a beanbag does.

To adjust the tablet viewing angle, you must reshape the pillow--it isn't enough to simply roll the pillow forward or backwards. Because the pillow is so firm, you must exert some effort in reshaping. It is easier to adjust the pillow shape and the viewing angle if you unzip the zipper that runs alongside the handle-tray, but then the pillow kind of flops around. (The zipper is there to open and close a compartment that is probably intended to hold your tablet, because the LAP PRO is also supposed to be a "caddy".)

If I needed a travel pillow (another of the LAP PRO's advertised uses) or a tablet caddy, I might end up liking the LAP PRO. However, because the stand is too large for convenient tabletop use, is hard to adjust, doesn't hold the tablet securely, and needs break-in time, I rate it at 2 stars ("I don't like it" on the official Amazon scale).

EDITED 11/18/12: After hearing from the seller, Renegade Concepts, I believe that I may have received an overfilled LAP PRO. (Renegade Concepts offered to replace my unit.) If my LAP PRO had been less firm out of the box, I would have rated it at 3 stars ("It's OK").
text_fidelity_b: Renegade Concepts: Lap PRO - Stand/Caddy Universal Beanbag Lap Stand Tablet Accessory for iPad 1, iPad 2, iPad 3, iPad 4, Acer, Nexus & All Android Tablets, E-Readers, Books & Google Devices (Blue)
